name: Ivan Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a carton folder-gluer and watch the flap seams at the stacker. After eighteen years I know the sounds of a bad guide, and I have a vocational certificate in machine operation. The glue smell follows me home, which my grown children still tease me about.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Vera works part-time at a flower shop, and our grown children live on their own. My operator wage is low, we rent and have less than a month saved, and there are few similar factories nearby. I have never used an AI tool; I would rather have someone show me a machine than follow a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the clever software can save the office a few minutes, but folded cartons still need a person watching the glue line. I have run this folder-gluer for eighteen years and I would rather fix a skewed seam than debate a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wage is low for an experienced operator, and my partner Vera only has part-time hours at a flower shop. We have three weeks of expenses saved and very few factories nearby; a quiet AI year still leaves me watching every bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would work the same gluer shift and put a small fixed amount from each new pay packet into savings before we buy extras. I would ask our union representative about the next pay meeting, because the present wage has not caught up with the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious even if AI fizzles. A single lost gluer shift or a week without my partner’s flower-shop pay would use our reserve before month ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a skewed seam look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flap overlaps by a finger width and the carton jams at the stacker. I stop the gluer and reset the guide before the next bundle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why speak to the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have a bargaining meeting next month. I want the operator wage and shift allowance on the agenda, not a rumour in the break room.

say: I would keep **carton seams** straight on the gluer.
I would put **operator wages** on the union meeting agenda.
think: Our **three-week reserve** cannot absorb one missed gluer shift and the next rent bill.
Vera’s **flower-shop hours** are part-time and could change at short notice.
do: Keep **folder-gluer shifts** and reset skewed seams.
Save a **small fixed amount** from each new pay packet.
Raise **operator wages** with the union representative at the next meeting.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary bills despite little AI change.
S0.quote: A single lost gluer shift or a week without my partner’s flower-shop pay would use our reserve before month ends.
fieldNote: His **low operator wage** leaves thin savings despite long experience.
The **union wage meeting** is a real group route he already knows, not a promise of a raise.

steps.text: Keep running folder-gluer and correcting skewed seams
Save a fixed amount from each new pay packet
Raise operator wages at next union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that the office can automate buying and schedules, but a robot needs time before it can pull a glued carton out of a jam. Workers should see the rota before anyone calls that progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first change might be software setting faster targets, then a robot stacker could take the second operator’s hours. We barely cover rent as it is, and there is no line of similar plants down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union representative to bring the proposed rota to a crew meeting. If management offers an actual paid guarded stacker trial, I would watch with the fitter, though I would not change controls myself without instruction; if hours are cut, I would apply for posted local operator work only where pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the rota. I know the gluer, but I do not want to learn a dangerous new stacker from a phone video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you join the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there is a paid place and a fitter has locked out the stacker first. A request for a demonstration does not mean I have agreed to run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far could you travel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bus to the next industrial park takes forty minutes. A job there has to leave enough pay after fare and hours lost to cover rent.

say: I would ask for a **crew rota meeting** before the stacker arrives.
I would keep **guarded trials** with a fitter, if offered.
think: Faster targets and a robot stacker could cut **my paid hours** on the gluer.
Few **nearby plants** leave little room for a bad offer after bus fares.
do: Ask **union representative** for a crew meeting on the proposed rota.
Attend **paid guarded stacker trial** only if offered and fitter isolates it.
Apply after **hour cuts** only for posted local bill-covering net-pay work.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic hour cuts and unsafe rushed instruction.
S1.quote: I do not want to learn a dangerous new stacker from a phone video.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **office automation** from slower physical stackers.
A paid demonstration is **conditional on an offer** and does not make him a qualified stacker operator.

steps.text: Ask union representative for crew meeting on proposed rota
Attend offered paid guarded stacker trial with fitter
Apply after cuts for posted local bill-covering net-pay operator job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union that thinking AGI in 2028, when I am sixty, would change buying and rosters first. By 2031, when I am sixty-three, capable robots could handle the carton jams and stacker work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the plant to drop a whole gluer shift once robots can work the line. I have less than a month saved, Vera’s flower-shop pay is part-time, and the few nearby plants might be making the same cuts; I am lying awake over the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union for written shift and severance terms and cut our paid television package now. I would apply for posted local machine or warehouse jobs that leave enough pay after bus fares for rent and food before giving notice; if the shift actually ends with no adequate offer, I would ask the housing office what help is available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed. I can repair a glue nozzle with my eyes half shut, but I cannot mend a missing wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot call it retirement while rent is due. I need actual pension and household figures before choosing a last shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union ask first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need a dated rota and written severance terms. I would not treat a meeting as protection until the plant puts its plan on paper.

say: I would demand **dated shift plans** before a whole gluer crew loses work.
I would make **severance terms** a union issue at the next bargaining meeting.
think: A whole **gluer shift** is likely to go around 2031.
Thin savings and **few factories** make the lost wage severe.
do: Request **written rota and severance** through the union.
Cancel **paid television** and search posted bill-covering local work.
Ask **housing office** about support if shift ends without adequate offer.
feel: **Alarmed** and losing sleep over an expected shift loss.
S2.quote: I can repair a glue nozzle with my eyes half shut, but I cannot mend a missing wage.
fieldNote: He expects **major paid shift loss** once robots handle jams around age sixty-three.
His **rent and thin reserve** make union documents, a careful job search and possible housing help material.

steps.text: Request dated rota and severance terms through union
Cancel paid television package to protect rent
Apply for posted local bill-covering net-pay machine or warehouse job before notice
Ask housing office for available help if shift ends without adequate offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that AGI in 2031 reaches our purchasing office when I am sixty-three, and hands-on robots around 2034 reach the glue line when I am sixty-six. Three years is something, if the factory uses it for workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not take to new screens quickly. A mechanical maintenance certificate might suit my hands, but a class fee or unpaid mornings would take rent money; I also need an actual local opening that pays enough after the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the gluer while shifts exist and ask the union to bargain for a funded course on paid time. If I am offered a place with supervised isolated-machine practice and there is a posted reachable maintenance job at bill-covering net pay, I would enrol and then apply after qualifying; without that place, I would search posted operator openings if hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, with time to test whether the course and the wage are real. I will not spend rent on a certificate that leads to an empty noticeboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could supervise practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our fitter Lina could show the stopped drive after it is isolated, if management gives her paid time. I would not touch a live belt for a training photograph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn AI controls instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI tool and do not want to guess at one on a running gluer. A properly taught mechanical course is the change I could manage.

say: I would press for **paid mechanical training** through the union.
I would keep **gluer shifts** while the line pays.
think: Unpaid class hours would eat **rent money** before he completes any certificate.
A **real maintenance vacancy** with adequate wages must justify the certificate.
do: Keep **gluer shifts** while paid work remains.
Enrol only in **funded course** with offered paid safe practice and adequate posted job.
Apply after **qualification** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay maintenance work.
feel: **Anxious**, but willing to consider a concrete mechanical route.
S3.quote: I will not spend rent on a certificate that leads to an empty noticeboard.
fieldNote: Resistance to **AI screens** does not rule out taught mechanical work.
Retraining needs an **offered funded paid place**, isolated practical instruction and a posted adequate local job.

steps.text: Keep paid folder-gluer shifts while available
Enrol if offered funded paid safe maintenance place and adequate posted job
Apply after qualification for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay maintenance job
Search posted operator jobs after cuts if no course place opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight, while capable robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. A long warning is useful only if an operator can afford to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had thought I might finish factory work around sixty-seven, but our three-week reserve and rent make that a hope, not a funded date. I do not know what any pension would actually pay, and Vera’s flower-shop hours cannot be promised ten years ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the gluer shift and put a small amount from each new wage into savings. I would request actual pension and rent figures; if verified household income covers housing, food and health costs at sixty-seven, I would leave factory work then, but if it does not I would continue safe paid work, and in the first year after 2036 I would check posted local jobs only if I am still employed and my hours are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about having to work longer than my hands can manage. I need a real income number before I tell the factory my last day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your hands cannot do the gluer then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask about lighter paid work and compare actual posted wages after travel. I cannot live on an assumption that a pension starts or covers our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children pay the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They are grown and have their own households. I would rather ask them for a lift to an appointment than put our bills on them.

say: I would demand **real retirement figures** before naming my last shift.
I would tell my grown children **2036 AGI** precedes 2039 robots.
think: Our **three-week reserve** cannot fund an early end to factory wages.
The **age-sixty-seven hope** depends on verified income for rent, food and health costs.
do: Keep **2026 gluer shifts** and save a little from new wages.
Leave **factory work at sixty-seven** only if verified income covers basic costs.
If still employed after **2036 cuts**, compare posted reachable bill-covering net-pay jobs.
feel: **Anxious** about having to work beyond his physical limits.
S4.quote: I need a real income number before I tell the factory my last day.
fieldNote: A **normal planned exit** at sixty-seven is conditional, with no pension entitlement presumed.
Current **2026 factory work** and possible post-2036 work are separate branches set by real income and hours.

steps.text: Save a little from each fresh 2026 wage
Leave factory at planned sixty-seven only if verified household income covers essentials
Compare posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work after cuts if still employed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots around 2031 could take the gluer shift before I can build savings. A written rota, paid safe training, and real local wages after travel would help more than a promise about new jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays rent while a worker learns a new machine. I have repaired more cartons than I can count, but repair skill cannot pay a missed week of wages.

headlineQuote: I have repaired more cartons than I can count, but repair skill cannot pay a missed week of wages.
portrait: **Ivan**, 58, is an experienced mid-level carton folder-gluer operator with average skill and a vocational machine certificate.
His **low wage**, Vera’s part-time flower-shop pay, grown children, rent, three-week reserve and few nearby factories constrain choices.
He has **never used AI**, favours union bargaining and would consider mechanical retraining only through funded paid safe practice.
Fast **2031 robots** could remove his shift; a planned age-sixty-seven exit requires verified household income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because 2031 robots may end the gluer shift while rent still needs wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **written rota**, offered funded safe paid training and posted local bill-covering net wages would help.
